subject: Forestry
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a 2-hour practical paper of four compulsory questions (60 marks); school candidates work with real specimens, tools and field data, while private candidates take an alternative-to-practical test. Questions ask you to identify trees, wildlife signs, tools and forest products, describe nursery, plantation, harvesting and processing procedures, interpret log markings and carry out mensuration calculations such as height, diameter, basal area and volume.

practicals.title: Identifying wildlife from tracks, droppings and features
practicals.topic: Practical: introduction to wildlife and plant identification
practicals.aim: To identify wildlife species from footprints, tracks, droppings, size, form and external features, describe their habitats, and calculate an encounter rate along a transect.
apparatus: Field guide to West African mammals and birds
materials: Mounted or photographed specimens (e.g. grasscutter, duiker, bushbuck, monkey, pangolin, hornbill, tortoise)
safety: Walk in groups with a guide; wear boots and long trousers against snakes and thorns.
Do not touch droppings with bare hands.
Never approach or provoke wild animals.
procedure: Walk slowly along a marked transect (e.g. a 3 km forest path) with the teacher or forest guard.
Look for signs: footprints, trails, droppings, feeding remains, nests, burrows, calls and sightings.
Measure the length and width of footprints and note the number of toes and presence of hoof or claw marks.
Photograph or cast clear footprints with plaster of Paris.
Identify the animal using the field guide and record the habitat where the sign was found.
Count all signs of one species along the transect and calculate the encounter rate.
Classify the species as common, rare or endangered.
practicals.expectedObservations: Duikers leave small paired (cloven) hoof prints and pellet droppings; the grasscutter (cane rat) leaves cut grass stems and runways in grassland; monkeys leave half-eaten fruits under trees; pangolins leave digging marks at termite mounds.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Encounter rate = number of signs ÷ transect length. Worked example: 18 duiker dropping groups are counted along a 3 km transect. Encounter rate = 18 ÷ 3 = 6 dropping groups per km. Comparing this rate between seasons or forests shows changes in relative abundance.
precautions: Count each sign once only.
Walk at a steady pace and keep the same search width.
Record signs immediately in the notebook.
commonMistakes: Confusing indirect signs (droppings) with sightings.
Calling the pangolin a reptile — it is a mammal with scales.
examTips: Give the habitat and one feature that identifies each animal.
Name endangered species correctly, e.g. pangolin, African elephant, chimpanzee, Cross River gorilla.
Include the unit 'per km' in encounter rates.

checkQuestions.explanation: Duikers are small antelopes with cloven hooves.

checkQuestions.explanation: The pangolin is covered with keratin scales.

checkQuestions.explanation: Signs such as calls, droppings and tracks are indirect evidence.

practicals.title: Identifying trees by leaves, bark, buttress and stem
practicals.aim: To identify common Nigerian timber and plantation trees from leaves, bark, slash, buttress and stem form, give local, trade and scientific names, and convert girth to diameter.
apparatus: Cutlass or bark knife (for a small slash)
materials: Trees on campus or in a nearby reserve, e.g. Iroko (Milicia excelsa), Obeche/Arere (Triplochiton scleroxylon), African mahogany (Khaya ivorensis), Teak (Tectona grandis), Gmelina (Gmelina arborea), Ceiba (Ceiba pentandra), Afara (Terminalia superba)
safety: Make only a small bark slash with care; keep the cutlass pointed away from people.
Watch for falling branches and stinging insects.
procedure: Observe the whole tree: crown shape, stem form, buttresses, height class.
Examine the leaves: simple or compound, arrangement, shape, margin, venation, hairs; collect a fallen leaf.
Examine the bark: colour, texture (smooth, scaly, fissured) and the colour and smell of a small slash; note any exudate (latex, gum, resin).
Measure the girth at breast height (1.3 m above ground) and calculate the diameter.
Use the key to name the tree, writing the scientific name correctly (genus with a capital letter, species in small letters, both underlined or in italics).
Record features and names in a table.
practicals.expectedObservations: Iroko has a cylindrical bole and its slash exudes white latex; Obeche has large plank buttresses and a soft pale wood; Teak has very large, rough leaves with a sandpaper feel; Ceiba has conical spines on young bark and large buttresses; Gmelina has heart-shaped leaves and yellow fruits.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Diameter = girth ÷ π. Worked example: an Iroko tree has a girth of 314 cm at breast height. Diameter = 314 ÷ 3.142 ≈ 99.9 cm ≈ 1.0 m.
precautions: Measure girth at exactly 1.3 m and above any buttress; keep the tape horizontal and tight.
Use several features together — one feature alone can mislead.
commonMistakes: Writing scientific names without capitalising the genus or with both names capitalised.
Measuring girth at ground level.
examTips: Give the scientific name in the correct binomial form, underlined when handwritten.
Two or three precise features per tree earn full marks (e.g. 'white latex from slash').
Indicate whether the species is indigenous or exotic (Teak and Gmelina are exotic).

A tree with girth 220 cm has a diameter of about

checkQuestions.explanation: Genus capitalised, species in lower case.

checkQuestions.explanation: Breast height is standardised at 1.3 m above ground.

practicals.title: Forestry tools, equipment and machinery
practicals.aim: To identify, use and maintain forestry and wildlife tools and machines, state their advantages and disadvantages, and prepare fuel for a two-stroke chainsaw.
safety: Wear personal protective equipment: helmet with visor and ear muffs, gloves, chainsaw trousers and steel-toe boots.
Mix fuel outdoors away from flames.
Start a chainsaw on the ground with the chain brake on.
procedure: Name each tool and classify it as nursery, plantation, mensuration, harvesting or wildlife tool.
State the use of each tool and demonstrate safe handling.
State two maintenance practices for each tool (sharpening, oiling, cleaning, tightening, proper storage).
Measure petrol and two-stroke oil in the correct ratio for the chainsaw and mix in a clean labelled container.
Check the chain tension and sharpness before use.
List advantages and disadvantages of manual tools versus machines.
practicals.expectedObservations: Hand tools are cheap and simple but slow and tiring; machines such as chainsaws are fast but expensive, noisy and dangerous without training.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Fuel mix: oil = petrol volume ÷ ratio. Worked example: the manufacturer recommends 50 : 1. For 5 L (5 000 mL) of petrol, oil = 5 000 ÷ 50 = 100 mL.
precautions: Keep cutting edges sharp — blunt tools need more force and cause accidents.
Store tools dry and oiled to prevent rust.
Never refuel a hot chainsaw.
sourcesOfError: Measuring oil roughly by eye gives a wrong mixture that damages the engine.
commonMistakes: Using four-stroke oil or no oil in chainsaw petrol.
Giving 'cleaning' as the only maintenance practice.
examTips: Pair each tool with one specific use and one specific maintenance practice.
Mention PPE when asked about safety with machines.

The Haga altimeter is used to measure
checkQuestions.explanation: It measures height from angles to the top and base.

options: is expensive and needs skilled maintenance
checkQuestions.explanation: Chainsaws are costly and require training and fuel.

checkQuestions.explanation: They contain fibres that jam the chain.

practicals.title: Seed collection, testing and sowing in the nursery
practicals.aim: To collect, store, treat and test tree seeds, carry out a germination test, and calculate the number of seeds to sow for a target number of seedlings.
materials: Seeds of e.g. Gmelina arborea, Tectona grandis, Leucaena leucocephala, Khaya
safety: Take care with boiling water during hot-water treatment.
Wear gloves when handling fungicide-treated seeds.
procedure: Collect mature fruits from healthy, well-formed mother trees; extract, clean and dry the seeds.
Store dry seeds in airtight labelled containers in a cool place.
Treat hard-coated seeds to break dormancy: soak in hot water and allow to cool overnight, or nick (scarify) the seed coat; soak Teak fruits in water for several days.
Place 100 treated seeds on moist filter paper or sand and keep moist.
Count germinated seeds daily for 14–21 days and calculate the germination percentage.
Sow seeds in beds or pots at a depth of about twice the seed's thickness and water lightly.
Calculate the number of seeds needed for the planting target.
practicals.expectedObservations: Treated hard-coated seeds swell and germinate sooner and more evenly than untreated seeds.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Germination % = germinated ÷ sown × 100. Seeds needed = target ÷ (germination fraction × survival fraction). Worked example: 72 of 100 seeds germinate → 72 %. To raise 5 000 plantable seedlings with 85 % nursery survival: 5 000 ÷ (0.72 × 0.85) ≈ 8 170 seeds.
precautions: Use a large random sample of seeds for testing.
Keep the germination medium moist but not waterlogged.
Label every batch with species and date.
sourcesOfError: Uneven moisture and temperature in trays.
Damping-off killing seedlings before they are counted.
commonMistakes: Sowing seeds too deep.
Forgetting to allow for losses when calculating seed needs.
examTips: Name a dormancy-breaking method suited to a named species.
Round seed numbers up — you cannot sow part of a seed.

options: soften the hard seed coat and break dormancy

practicals.title: Nursery bed preparation, pricking out and hardening off
practicals.aim: To prepare nursery beds and potting mixture, prick out and transplant seedlings, harden them off, and calculate seed purity and the number of pots on a bed.
apparatus: Shade frame (palm fronds or shade net)
materials: Topsoil, river sand and well-rotted manure
safety: Lift soil bags correctly.
Wash hands after handling manure.
procedure: Choose a level, well-drained site near water and clear it.
Prepare beds about 1 m wide with paths between them; erect shade over the beds.
Mix topsoil, sand and manure (e.g. 3 : 1 : 1), sieve and fill polythene pots; arrange them upright on the bed.
Prick out seedlings at the two-leaf stage by lifting with a dibber, holding the leaf (not the stem), and plant one per pot.
Water morning and evening, weed regularly and protect from pests.
Harden off by gradually removing shade and reducing watering 2–4 weeks before field planting.
Determine seed purity of a seed lot and count the seeds per kilogram.
practicals.expectedObservations: Pricked-out seedlings wilt slightly for a day and recover; hardened-off seedlings have tougher, darker leaves and woody stems.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Purity % = pure seed mass ÷ sample mass × 100; seeds per kg = seeds in sample ÷ sample mass (g) × 1 000. Worked example: a 50 g sample contains 46 g of pure seed (purity = 92 %) and 1 250 seeds (1 250 ÷ 50 × 1 000 = 25 000 seeds/kg). Pots per bed: a 10 m × 1 m bed holding pots 10 cm across in rows takes 100 × 10 = 1 000 pots.
precautions: Hold seedlings by the leaves to avoid damaging the stem.
Prick out in the cool of the day.
Do not over-water — it encourages damping-off.
sourcesOfError: Impurities such as broken seeds not separated carefully.
commonMistakes: Removing shade suddenly instead of gradually.
Leaving pots half-filled so they collapse.
examTips: Define pricking out, hardening off, stumping and beating up precisely.
Distinguish permanent from temporary (flying) nurseries.

checkQuestions.q: Hardening off means
options: gradually exposing seedlings to field conditions

practicals.title: Costing a tree nursery
practicals.aim: To group the costs of a tree nursery into direct and indirect costs, calculate the total cost and the cost per plantable seedling, and suggest ways of controlling costs.
materials: Nursery records or a given cost table
safety: No special hazards; keep records secure and accurate.
procedure: List all nursery expenses for the season.
Group them into direct costs (seeds, pots, soil, labour, tools) and indirect costs (stationery, maintenance, rent of plot).
Total each group and add to find the total cost.
Count the number of plantable seedlings produced.
Divide the total cost by the number of seedlings to obtain the unit cost.
Suggest ways of reducing cost, e.g. using family labour, local materials and reducing seedling losses.
practicals.expectedObservations: Labour and pots usually form the largest share of direct costs; losses in the nursery raise the cost per seedling.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: direct costs — seeds ₦15 000, 5 000 pots at ₦20 = ₦100 000, topsoil ₦40 000, labour ₦180 000, tools ₦45 000 → ₦380 000. Indirect costs — stationery ₦10 000, maintenance ₦25 000, rent ₦35 000 → ₦70 000. Total = ₦450 000. With 90 % survival of 5 000 seedlings = 4 500 plantable seedlings, cost per seedling = 450 000 ÷ 4 500 = ₦100.
precautions: Record every expense with date and receipt.
Do not count the same item under both direct and indirect costs.
commonMistakes: Dividing by seedlings sown rather than seedlings that survived.
Treating plot rent as a direct cost.
examTips: Show subtotals for direct and indirect costs before the grand total.
Write currency signs and units throughout.

checkQuestions.q: Which of these is an indirect nursery cost?
checkQuestions.explanation: Rent is an overhead not tied to each seedling.

checkQuestions.q: A nursery costs ₦240 000 and produces 3 000 plantable seedlings. Cost per seedling is
Reducing seedling mortality lowers the cost per seedling because
options: the same total cost is shared among more seedlings
checkQuestions.explanation: Unit cost = total cost ÷ number produced.

practicals.title: Controlling nursery pests and diseases
practicals.aim: To identify common nursery pests and diseases (e.g. damping-off, termites, crickets, leaf-eating caterpillars), measure the level of damage and apply control measures correctly.
safety: Wear protective clothing when mixing and spraying chemicals.
Spray in still air, not against the wind.
Keep chemicals away from children and food.
procedure: Inspect seedlings and record symptoms: collapsed stems at soil level (damping-off), chewed leaves, cut stems, wilting, leaf spots.
Identify the pest or disease and its cause.
Count the total and affected seedlings and calculate the percentage mortality.
Remove and destroy diseased seedlings.
Mix fungicide or insecticide at the label rate and spray evenly.
Adjust cultural practices: reduce watering, improve drainage, thin crowded seedlings, sterilise soil.
practicals.expectedObservations: Damping-off seedlings have water-soaked, shrunken stems at soil level and fall over; termite damage shows ringbarked stems with soil tunnels.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Mortality % = dead seedlings ÷ total × 100; chemical = rate × volume. Worked example: 84 of 1 200 seedlings are killed by damping-off → 84 ÷ 1 200 × 100 = 7 %. Fungicide at 2 g per litre for a 15 L knapsack = 2 × 15 = 30 g.
precautions: Follow the label dosage exactly.
Wash the sprayer after use.
Avoid over-watering and overcrowding, which favour damping-off.
sourcesOfError: Counting seedlings that died from drought as diseased.
commonMistakes: Spraying fungicide to control insects.
Leaving dead seedlings in the bed.
examTips: Name the causal organism type (damping-off is caused by soil fungi such as Pythium).
Combine cultural and chemical control in answers.

checkQuestions.q: Damping-off of seedlings is caused by
checkQuestions.explanation: Fungi such as Pythium attack the stem at soil level.

checkQuestions.q: 45 of 900 seedlings die. Mortality is
A cultural method of reducing damping-off is
checkQuestions.explanation: The fungi thrive in wet, crowded conditions.

practicals.title: Planning, surveying and pegging a plantation
practicals.topic: Practical: plantation establishment and land preparation
practicals.aim: To lay out a plantation plot, peg planting positions at a given espacement, plant seedlings correctly and calculate the number of seedlings required.
safety: Wear boots and gloves when clearing.
Carry tools safely and keep a distance between workers.
procedure: Survey the site, draw a plan showing compartments, roads and firebreaks.
Clear the site by slashing; remove stumps along lines if necessary.
Establish a straight base line with ranging poles; set out a right angle (3-4-5 method) for the second side.
Use a marked rope to peg planting points at the chosen spacing (e.g. 3 m × 3 m).
Dig planting holes (about 30 cm × 30 cm × 30 cm), remove the polythene pot, plant at the root-collar level and firm the soil.
Record the number planted and the date; replace dead seedlings later (beating up).
practicals.expectedObservations: Pegs in straight rows and columns form a square grid; correctly planted seedlings stand upright with the root collar at ground level.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Seedlings = area ÷ (spacing × spacing). Worked example: 2 ha (20 000 m²) at 3 m × 3 m → 20 000 ÷ 9 ≈ 2 222 seedlings; adding 10 % for beating up → 2 222 × 1.1 ≈ 2 445 seedlings to raise.
precautions: Remove the polythene pot before planting.
Plant at the onset of the rains.
Keep lines straight for easy tending.
sourcesOfError: Slopes increase the true distance between pegs.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert hectares to square metres (1 ha = 10 000 m²).
Planting too deep or leaving roots exposed.
examTips: Show the area conversion step.
Name the 3-4-5 method for setting right angles.

checkQuestions.q: How many seedlings are needed for 1 ha at 2.5 m × 2.5 m?

checkQuestions.explanation: A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 has a right angle.

practicals.title: Tending: weeding, beating up, pruning and thinning
practicals.aim: To carry out tending operations in a young plantation and calculate survival percentage, beating-up requirements and thinning numbers.
safety: Prune above head height only with a pole saw and helmet.
Keep away from falling branches.
procedure: Ring-weed around each tree (about 1 m radius) and slash between rows.
Count living and dead trees and calculate the survival percentage.
Beat up (replace dead seedlings) early in the rainy season.
Prune lower branches flush with the branch collar to produce clear, knot-free timber.
Select trees for thinning (suppressed, diseased, crooked), mark them with paint and remove them.
Record all operations and dates.
practicals.expectedObservations: Ring-weeded trees grow faster; pruned stems are clean; thinned stands have wider crowns and larger diameter growth.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: 1 ha at 3 m × 3 m = 10 000 ÷ 9 ≈ 1 111 trees planted; 950 alive → survival = 950 ÷ 1 111 × 100 ≈ 85.5 %; trees to beat up = 1 111 − 950 = 161. A 40 % thinning of the 950 trees removes 0.4 × 950 = 380 trees.
precautions: Do not leave stubs when pruning; do not cut into the branch collar.
Thin in stages, not all at once.
sourcesOfError: Trees hidden by weeds may be missed in counts.
commonMistakes: Confusing beating up (replacing dead seedlings) with thinning (removing living trees).
Pruning live branches too heavily, slowing growth.
examTips: Give the reason for each tending operation.
Show survival as a percentage of trees planted.

checkQuestions.explanation: Removing lower branches gives clear boles.

checkQuestions.explanation: Poor trees are removed to favour the best.

practicals.title: Measuring tree height with a clinometer and Haga altimeter
practicals.aim: To determine the height of a standing tree using a clinometer (trigonometric method) and a Haga altimeter.
materials: A standing tree on level ground
safety: Look out for dead branches overhead.
Do not walk backwards over uneven ground without checking behind.
procedure: Choose a point from which both the base and the top of the tree are visible, on level ground.
Measure the horizontal distance from this point to the base of the tree (e.g. 20 m).
Measure your eye height above the ground.
Sight the tree top with the clinometer and read the angle of elevation.
Calculate the height using trigonometry and add the eye height.
Repeat with a Haga altimeter set to the matching distance scale (15, 20, 25 or 30 m), reading the top and base and adding them.
Take readings from two positions and find the mean.
practicals.expectedObservations: The height from the clinometer and Haga altimeter should agree within about 0.5–1 m.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Height = distance × tan(angle) + eye height. Worked example: distance 20 m, angle 35°, eye height 1.5 m. tan 35° = 0.7002; 20 × 0.7002 = 14.0 m; height = 14.0 + 1.5 = 15.5 m.
precautions: Measure distance horizontally.
Stand at a distance roughly equal to the tree height for best accuracy.
Sight the true top, not a side branch.
sourcesOfError: Difficulty seeing the top in dense canopy.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to add eye height.
Using sin or cos instead of tan.
Calculator set to radians instead of degrees.
examTips: Draw a labelled right-angled triangle — it often earns a mark.
Give the answer to one decimal place with the unit m.

checkQuestions.explanation: When the base is below eye level, add the readings: 15.0 + 1.5.

practicals.title: Diameter, girth and basal area of trees
practicals.aim: To measure the diameter at breast height (dbh) and girth of trees with a diameter tape and calliper, and to calculate basal area and standing volume.
safety: Beware of ants, wasps and thorns on tree stems.
procedure: Use the 1.3 m stick to mark breast height on each tree on the uphill side.
Wrap the diameter tape horizontally around the stem at 1.3 m, pull it tight and read girth (or diameter directly on the d-side).
Measure the diameter with a calliper in two directions at right angles and average them.
Calculate diameter from girth, then basal area.
Combine basal area with height and a form factor to estimate tree volume.
Record results with conventional symbols: d (dbh), g (basal area), h (height), v (volume).
practicals.expectedObservations: Calliper and tape diameters agree closely on round stems; oval stems give different calliper readings in two directions.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: d = girth ÷ π; basal area g = πd²/4; volume v = g × h × f. Worked example: girth 157 cm → d = 157 ÷ 3.142 = 50.0 cm = 0.50 m; g = 3.142 × 0.50² ÷ 4 = 0.196 m². With h = 20 m and form factor 0.5: v = 0.196 × 20 × 0.5 ≈ 1.96 m³.
precautions: Convert cm to m before calculating basal area in m².
Measure above buttresses or swellings if they occur at 1.3 m.
Keep the tape horizontal.
commonMistakes: Using girth instead of diameter in πd²/4.
Forgetting to square the diameter.
Mixing cm and m.
examTips: Write the formula, substitution and unit (m², m³) at each step.
State the meaning of conventional symbols when asked.

checkQuestions.q: The basal area of a tree of dbh 40 cm is about
Basal area is the cross-sectional area of a tree at
checkQuestions.explanation: It is measured at breast height.

practicals.title: Calculating log volume with Smalian's and Huber's formulae
practicals.aim: To measure the length and end and middle diameters of a log and calculate its volume using Smalian's and Huber's formulae.
materials: Felled logs at a timber depot or sawmill
safety: Never stand on the downhill side of a log; chock logs so they cannot roll.
Wear boots and gloves.
procedure: Measure the length of the log along its axis.
Measure the diameter at the base (large end) and the top (small end) in two directions; average each.
Mark the midpoint and measure the mid-diameter.
Calculate the cross-sectional areas.
Apply Smalian's formula V = L(Ab + At)/2 and Huber's formula V = L × Am.
Compare the two results.
practicals.expectedObservations: Smalian's formula usually gives a slightly larger volume than Huber's for tapering logs.
precautions: Measure diameters under bark if the question requires it.
Take two diameters at right angles at each point and average.
sourcesOfError: Irregular log shape and end damage.
commonMistakes: Averaging the diameters instead of the areas in Smalian's formula.
Mixing units (cm and m).
examTips: Name the formula used; write the units m² and m³.
Give answers to three decimal places when the numbers allow.

practicals.title: Enumeration of growing stock by sampling
practicals.topic: Enumeration of growing stock and sampling methods
practicals.aim: To carry out a sample enumeration (e.g. 5 %) of a forest compartment using systematic sample plots, and estimate the number of trees and volume for the whole compartment.
safety: Work in teams and agree on meeting points.
Carry first aid and water.
procedure: Decide the enumeration intensity (100 %, 5 % or 2 %) and calculate the area to be sampled.
Lay out sample plots or strips systematically (at fixed intervals) or randomly on the map, then locate them in the field with compass and tape.
In each plot, identify every tree above the minimum dbh, measure dbh (and height for sample trees) and paint-mark it.
Tally the trees by species and diameter class.
Calculate the total number and volume in the sample area.
Expand the sample results to the whole compartment by dividing by the sampling fraction.
practicals.expectedObservations: Systematic plots spread evenly across the compartment; tally sheets show more small trees than large ones in natural forest.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Estimate = sample value ÷ sampling fraction. Worked example: compartment 40 ha, 5 % enumeration → 40 × 0.05 = 2 ha sampled. Trees ≥ 60 cm dbh counted = 36 with volume 90 m³. Estimated total = 36 ÷ 0.05 = 720 trees and 90 ÷ 0.05 = 1 800 m³.
precautions: Mark trees to avoid counting them twice.
Keep plot boundaries accurate.
Use the same minimum diameter throughout.
sourcesOfError: Uneven distribution of trees makes small samples unrepresentative.
Boundary trees wrongly included or excluded.
commonMistakes: Multiplying by the sampling fraction instead of dividing.
Confusing systematic (fixed interval) with random sampling.
examTips: Define 100 %, 5 % and 2 % enumeration.
State one advantage each of systematic and random sampling.

practicals.title: Measuring slope and plot area in a forest survey
practicals.aim: To measure the angle and gradient of a slope with a clinometer, and the area of a forest plot by chain survey.
materials: A sloping area and a small plot
safety: Take care on steep slopes; wear boots with good grip.
procedure: Place ranging poles at the top and bottom of the slope.
Sight from eye height on one pole to the same height on the other pole with the clinometer and read the angle.
Measure the horizontal distance and the vertical rise (or calculate rise from the angle).
Calculate the gradient as a percentage and the angle.
For plot area, chain the boundaries, divide the plot into triangles and rectangles and record measurements in the field book.
Calculate the area and convert to hectares.
practicals.expectedObservations: Steeper slopes give larger clinometer angles; plantation plots on slopes above about 30 % need contour planting.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Gradient % = rise ÷ horizontal distance × 100; angle = tan⁻¹(rise ÷ distance). Worked example: rise 12 m over 80 m → 12 ÷ 80 × 100 = 15 %; angle = tan⁻¹(0.15) ≈ 8.5°. A rectangular plot 250 m × 120 m = 30 000 m² = 3 ha.
precautions: Keep the chain or tape horizontal (step chaining on slopes).
Sight to the same height as your eye on the target pole.
sourcesOfError: Misreading the clinometer scale (degrees v. percent).
commonMistakes: Confusing gradient percentage with degrees.
Forgetting 1 ha = 10 000 m².
examTips: State which scale (degrees or percent) the clinometer reading is on.
Show conversion to hectares.

practicals.title: Felling procedure and directional felling
practicals.aim: To describe and demonstrate (on a small tree, under supervision) the safe procedure for felling timber, including directional felling with a notch, hinge and back cut.
apparatus: Chainsaw or axe and cross-cut saw
materials: A small tree marked for felling
safety: Only trained persons fell trees; students observe from at least twice the tree height away.
Plan two escape routes at about 45° behind the tree.
Never fell in strong wind.
procedure: Check the tree's lean, crown weight, dead branches and surroundings; choose the felling direction.
Clear undergrowth around the base and prepare escape routes.
Cut the notch (face cut) on the side facing the felling direction, about one-quarter to one-third of the diameter deep.
Make the back cut on the opposite side slightly above the base of the notch, leaving a hinge about one-tenth of the diameter.
Insert wedges if needed; shout a warning and retreat along an escape route as the tree falls.
Delimb, cross-cut into logs and mark the stump and logs.
practicals.expectedObservations: The hinge guides the tree to fall in the direction of the notch; the stump shows the notch, hinge and back cut.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: tree diameter 80 cm, height 25 m. Notch depth = ¼ × 80 = 20 cm; hinge thickness = 10 % × 80 = 8 cm; danger zone radius = 2 × 25 = 50 m.
precautions: Never cut through the hinge.
Keep onlookers out of the danger zone.
Wear helmet, visor, ear protection, gloves and boots.
sourcesOfError: Hidden rot changes how the tree falls.
commonMistakes: Making the back cut below the notch.
Retreating directly behind the tree, where the butt may kick back.
examTips: List pre-felling activities: stock survey, marking, climber cutting, road planning.
State at least three safety measures.

checkQuestions.explanation: The tree falls towards the notch.

practicals.title: Interpreting log markings
practicals.aim: To read and interpret the markings on logs and stumps — property mark, locality mark, compartment number, stock survey number, tree number, reserve code and log number — and to relate logs to their tree.
materials: Marked logs at a timber depot or photographs of log ends
safety: Do not climb on log stacks.
Keep clear of loading machines.
procedure: Examine the end of each log and the corresponding stump.
Copy the markings exactly into the notebook.
Interpret each part of the marking using the key provided.
Check that the tree number on the log matches the stump.
Measure the logs and calculate the number of logs obtained from the tree.
State why log marking is important (ownership, control of illegal felling, revenue collection, tracing logs to source).
practicals.expectedObservations: A typical marking might read 'FD / OK-R / C12 / SS045 / T17 / L2', meaning Forestry Department property, Okomu reserve code, compartment 12, stock survey number 045, tree 17, log 2.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: tree 17 has a merchantable bole of 18 m cross-cut into 6 m logs → 18 ÷ 6 = 3 logs, marked L1, L2 and L3. A log marked L2 is the middle log of that tree.
precautions: Record markings exactly; a small error traces a log to the wrong tree.
Read both ends where possible.

practicals.title: Harvesting non-timber forest products sustainably
practicals.topic: Practical: methods of harvesting non-timber forest products
practicals.aim: To describe and observe methods of harvesting NTFPs — collection (snails, mushrooms), gathering (leaves, fruits, medicinal plants), hunting and trapping — and to distinguish sustainable from harmful practices.
materials: Specimens or photographs of giant African land snails, edible mushrooms, Gnetum (afang/okazi) leaves, bush mango (Irvingia) seeds, chewing sticks, rattan, honey
safety: Never eat wild mushrooms unless identified by an expert — some are deadly.
Wear gloves when collecting snails and handling bark.
procedure: List NTFPs found in the local forest and the method of harvesting each.
Collect snails at night or early morning after rain, taking only mature snails with a thickened shell lip.
Harvest leaves (e.g. Gnetum) by picking some leaves and leaving the growing tip so the plant regrows.
Weigh and grade harvested products.
Identify harmful practices: felling trees for fruit, ring-barking for medicine, bush burning for hunting, use of poison or dynamite in fishing, hunting in the closed season.
Suggest sustainable alternatives.
practicals.expectedObservations: Mature snails have a hard, thickened lip at the shell opening; immature snails have a thin, brittle lip.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: a collector gathers 40 snails averaging 150 g each = 40 × 150 = 6 000 g = 6 kg. If 25 % of them are immature and returned, 30 mature snails (4.5 kg) are kept.
precautions: Leave immature snails and some fruits to sustain the population.
Harvest bark in narrow strips on one side only.
Obey closed seasons and protected-species laws.
sourcesOfError: Mass varies with how much soil and moisture is on products.
commonMistakes: Listing timber as an NTFP.
Treating bush burning as an acceptable hunting method.
examTips: Give named examples of NTFPs with their uses.
For each harmful practice give one consequence (e.g. loss of species, soil degradation).

practicals.title: Timber processing: sawn timber, plywood and wood moisture
practicals.aim: To identify processed wood products (sawn timber, veneer, plywood, particle board, carvings), describe how they are made, and calculate sawmill recovery and moisture content of wood.
materials: Samples of sawn plank, veneer, plywood, particle board, fibreboard, wood carvings
Small wood blocks for moisture tests
safety: Keep away from moving saws at the sawmill; wear ear protection.
Use tongs with hot samples.
procedure: Examine each sample and note its structure: plywood has odd-numbered layers with grain at right angles; particle board is made of glued chips; veneer is a thin sheet.
Describe the processing steps: debarking, sawing (sawn timber), peeling or slicing (veneer), gluing and pressing (plywood, particle board), seasoning and preservative treatment.
Measure the boards produced from a log and calculate their volume.
Calculate the sawmill recovery percentage.
Weigh a fresh wood block, oven-dry to constant mass and reweigh; calculate moisture content.
practicals.expectedObservations: Plywood is strong in both directions because the grain alternates; fresh wood loses much mass on drying.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Board volume = length × width × thickness. Worked example: a 3.6 m × 0.30 m × 0.025 m board = 0.027 m³. If a 1.2 m³ log yields 0.66 m³ of boards, recovery = 0.66 ÷ 1.2 × 100 = 55 %. Moisture content (dry basis) = (wet − oven-dry) ÷ oven-dry × 100: wet 120 g, dry 80 g → 40 ÷ 80 × 100 = 50 %.
precautions: Dry samples to constant mass.
Convert all dimensions to metres before multiplying.
sourcesOfError: Sawdust and slabs not accounted for.
commonMistakes: Dividing by wet mass when moisture content on dry basis is asked.
Leaving thickness in mm.
examTips: State that seasoning reduces shrinkage, warping and fungal attack.
Name the layers and gluing in plywood manufacture.

options: thin veneers with grain at right angles

practicals.title: Processing and preserving non-timber forest products
practicals.topic: Practical: processing of non-timber forest products
practicals.aim: To identify NTFPs such as rattan, bamboo, mushrooms, snails, bushmeat and medicinal plants, describe their processing and preservation, and calculate drying losses.
safety: Cook bushmeat and snails thoroughly; never handle animals found dead.
Take care with knives and hot kilns.
procedure: Identify each NTFP and state its uses.
Rattan: scrape off the sheath, sun-dry, sort by diameter and bend with heat for furniture.
Bamboo: cut mature culms, soak or treat with preservative, then dry.
Mushrooms and leaves: clean, slice and dry in a solar dryer; store in airtight containers.
Snails and bushmeat: wash, boil or smoke, then store.
Weigh products before and after drying and calculate the moisture lost.
practicals.expectedObservations: Dried mushrooms become light and brittle and keep for months; treated bamboo resists borers.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Moisture lost % = (fresh − dry) ÷ fresh × 100. Worked example: 2.0 kg of fresh mushrooms dry to 0.2 kg; loss = 1.8 kg; 1.8 ÷ 2.0 × 100 = 90 %.
precautions: Dry in clean conditions protected from dust and flies.
Store dried products in airtight containers to prevent re-wetting and moulds.
sourcesOfError: Incomplete drying gives a high final mass and causes spoilage.
commonMistakes: Confusing rattan (a climbing palm) with bamboo (a grass).
Describing uses without processing.
examTips: For each product give one processing method and one preservation method.
Mention value addition and income generation.

practicals.title: Cultivating oyster mushrooms on sawdust
practicals.aim: To cultivate oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus) on a sawdust substrate, harvest them and calculate biological efficiency.
apparatus: PVC neck rings and cotton wool
safety: Take care with steam and hot drums.
Only eat mushrooms you have grown from known spawn.
procedure: Mix sawdust with about 10 % bran and 1 % lime; add water until a squeezed handful releases only a few drops.
Fill bags (about 1 kg dry substrate each), fit neck rings and plug with cotton wool.
Pasteurise or sterilise the bags by steaming for several hours and allow to cool.
Inoculate each bag with spawn under clean conditions.
Incubate in a dark place at about 25 °C until white mycelium covers the substrate (3–4 weeks).
Open the bags, mist with water two to three times daily in a humid, airy room.
Harvest mature fruiting bodies by twisting them off; weigh and record yields over several flushes.
practicals.expectedObservations: White cottony mycelium spreads through the bags; pin heads appear within a week of opening, growing into fan-shaped caps in 3–5 days; contaminated bags show green or black moulds.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Biological efficiency (BE) % = fresh mushroom mass ÷ dry substrate mass × 100. Worked example: 10 bags × 1 kg dry substrate = 10 kg; total yield = 6.5 kg fresh mushrooms. BE = 6.5 ÷ 10 × 100 = 65 %.
precautions: Work with clean hands and surfaces when spawning to avoid contamination.
Keep humidity high but avoid water pooling on caps.
Remove contaminated bags at once.
commonMistakes: Using fresh or aromatic sawdust that inhibits mycelium.
Exposing bags to light during spawn run.
examTips: Know the parts of a mushroom: cap (pileus), gills, stalk (stipe), mycelium.
List stages: substrate preparation, sterilisation, spawning, incubation, fruiting, harvesting.

practicals.title: Beekeeping: colony members, hive inspection and honey harvest
practicals.aim: To identify members of a honey bee colony and beekeeping equipment, describe hive inspection and honey harvesting and processing, and calculate honey yield.
apparatus: Kenyan top-bar hive or Langstroth hive
materials: Preserved queen, worker and drone bees
safety: Wear a full bee suit and veil; work in the evening or calm weather.
Students allergic to bee stings must not approach the hive.
Use smoke gently; never use fire directly on bees.
procedure: Examine and draw the queen, worker and drone; note differences in size, abdomen and eyes.
Light the smoker and puff smoke gently at the hive entrance.
Open the hive quietly; lift combs one at a time and check for brood, stores, queen cells and pests (e.g. wax moth, ants).
Select ripe honey combs that are at least three-quarters capped with wax.
Brush off the bees, cut out the comb and close the hive.
Extract honey by pressing or crushing and straining; allow it to settle, then bottle.
Melt the remaining comb in hot water to recover beeswax; weigh the products.
practicals.expectedObservations: The queen is the largest with a long abdomen; drones are stout with large eyes and no sting; workers are smallest and most numerous. Ripe honey combs are sealed with white wax caps.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: 10 top-bar combs averaging 1.2 kg each = 12 kg of comb. If honey is 75 % of comb mass, honey = 12 × 0.75 = 9 kg, which fills 9 ÷ 0.5 = 18 half-kilogram bottles.
precautions: Harvest only capped combs; uncapped honey ferments.
Leave enough honey for the colony.
Keep processing equipment clean and dry.
sourcesOfError: Comb mass includes some brood or pollen.
commonMistakes: Saying drones collect nectar (only workers do).
Using too much smoke, which can taint honey.
examTips: State the role of each colony member.
List bee products: honey, beeswax, propolis, royal jelly, pollen, venom.
Name the smoker and veil with their uses — commonly asked.
